title: What $100 Will Buy in 30 Years (Inflation Explained)
description:
At 3% inflation a year, $100 in cash buys about $74 of today's goods after 10 years, $55 after 20 and $41 after 30. To just keep up, that $100 has to grow to $134, $181 and $243.

Assumptions: a steady 3% inflation rate every year (a round number; actual inflation changes year to year). The US Federal Reserve's longer-run goal is 2% inflation, measured by the PCE price index (source: federalreserve.gov); at 2%, $100 buys about $55 of today's goods after 30 years.

scenes.say: Put a hundred dollar bill in a drawer. In thirty years, it'll only buy what forty-one dollars buys today.
That's with prices rising three percent a year. A simple round number. Real inflation changes every year.
After ten years, your hundred buys about seventy-four dollars of today's stuff. After twenty, fifty-five. After thirty, forty-one.
Flip it around. Just to keep up, that hundred has to grow to one thirty-four in ten years, one eighty-one in twenty, and two forty-three in thirty.
Even at the Federal Reserve's two percent target, thirty years cuts a hundred dollars down to about fifty-five.
So money you won't need for years has to grow at least as fast as prices, just to stand still.
